sources: Revised grammar plan — Weeks 1–4, syllabus aligned (21 Nov 2026)
Vocabulary review — Weeks 1–4, syllabus aligned (21 Nov 2026)

grammarTask.order: notice forms (2 min), meaning checks (2), choose (3), complete (3), fix (2), rewrite (2), light (2), own sentences with AI feedback (3), review (1)

pilotRules.speaking: Record 60–90 seconds. Hide the model before the first take. One specific AI correction, then record again straight away.
pilotRules.writing: 30 minutes, 120–150 words, instant AI feedback and revise-and-retry. A few days later a new speaking prompt without the phrase bank.
pilotRules.conversation: 15 minutes recommended; 3–4 turns with the AI partner on the week's theme, grammar and featured words. Feedback after the exchange, then one turn retried.
pilotRules.extensiveInput: About 60 minutes a week of graded B1 listening or reading with transcripts or captions, tagged to the week's theme; 40 minutes minimum; up to 5 personal words.
pilotRules.progression: No fixed days or deadlines. The next week opens when speaking, writing and either listening or reading are done.
pilotRules.level: Adults and older teenagers (16+) at secure B1. Adult contexts: work, flat-sharing, plans and travel. Judge control and clarity, not the number of forms used.
pilotRules.grammarClinic: Only syllabus B1 basics: present simple and continuous, articles, quantifiers, prepositions, subject–verb agreement and verb forms. Every Light point is taught in its own week, not moved to the clinic.

conversationRules.levelAndTurns: The partner speaks at B1 in one- or two-sentence turns and asks one follow-up per turn. Ends after 3–4 learner turns, or earlier on request.
conversationRules.errors: No interruption or mid-conversation corrections; natural recasts only, e.g. 'Oh, you've lived there since May?'
conversationRules.feedback: After the exchange: up to three corrections prioritising the week's grammar, one featured word used well or one that would have fitted, then one turn retried.
conversationRules.labelledAsAi: The partner and its feedback are always labelled as AI; learners can dispute feedback with 'I think this is right'.
conversationRules.accent: Feedback covers grammar, vocabulary and clarity. A Spanish or regional accent is never an error; misrecognised words are not grammar mistakes.
conversationRules.safety: Stays on the week's theme, declines romantic, sexual, harmful or personal-data topics, never asks for an address or phone number, suitable for ages 16–17, report button on every exchange, transcripts kept under the privacy policy.

weeks.title: A change you got used to
weeks.canDo: Tell a story about a change: set the scene, sequence events and connect them to now.

grammar.main: Use the past simple for finished events ('I moved last year'), the past continuous for background ('while I was walking home') and the past perfect for an earlier event ('I'd never run with a group before'). Use the present perfect for a change up to now ('Since then, I've made a few friends').
grammar.light: used to + infinitive for past habits and states; would + infinitive for repeated past actions only ('We would cook together on Sundays', not 'I would live in Leeds'). Present perfect continuous for an activity continuing up to now ('I've been running with the group for six months').

sampleItems.prompt: I ___ here last year. Since then, I've made a few friends.
When I was a child, we ___ in a small flat.
sampleItems.reason: 'Live' is a state, so would is not possible.

grammar.authoringNote: Would for past habits is not normally used in negatives, questions or states; accept used to or the past simple there, and don't flag the past simple where used to is possible. Contrast result ('I've made a few friends') and activity ('I've been running').

speaking.prompt: What was life like before? What changed, what was difficult, what helped, and what is different now? Listen to the model first, then hide it before recording.
speaking.model: When I moved to a new city last year, I didn't know anyone. In my old town, I used to see my friends every weekend, and we would often cook together on Sunday evenings. So the biggest challenge I faced was meeting people outside work. It took me a few weeks to get used to spending my evenings alone. One evening, while I was walking home, I saw a poster for a running group. I'd never run with a group before, so I was nervous at the first session, but I gradually got to know the other runners. Since then, I've made a few friends, and the city feels more like home. I've been running with the group for about six months now. When I look back on those first few weeks, I'm really glad I went to that first session.
speaking.b2Stretch: Explain why the change mattered and how you feel about it now, without the cue card.

writing.prompt: Write a personal narrative about a change. Set the scene, use since then or eventually to move the story on, and close with one sentence about how things are now.
writing.delayedRecall: Tell me about a new routine that felt strange at first. What helped it feel normal?

conversation.scenario: Catching up with an old friend.
conversation.openingLine: It's been ages! What's changed since I last saw you?
conversation.learnerMoves: Describe one change, what was hard and how life is now; answer one follow-up.
conversation.targetLanguage: Narrative tenses, present perfect vs past simple, used to / would; face a challenge, get used to, since then

core.example: I had to adapt to living abroad.
Moving to Leeds was a turning point in my life.
I faced several challenges while I was studying abroad.
It took me a month to get used to living alone.
When I look back on my first year abroad, I remember the people I met.
I've never regretted leaving my old job.
My English gradually improved while I was living in York.
Travelling alone was a memorable experience.

collocations.example: I made a big decision about my future.
I took a risk and applied for a job abroad.
I decided to make a change and cycle to work.
I've kept in touch with my old school friends.
I've been making good progress since September.
I took up photography after I moved.

families.card: decision is productive on the collocation card; decisive and indecisive recognition only

vocabulary.note: Teach get used to + noun or -ing for B1 production; contrast used to + infinitive on the same card. Keep adapt to as guided B2.

linkers.example: Eventually, I got used to it.
I moved in September. Since then, I've made some good friends.

checkpoint1.focus: Finished time, past-to-now, past continuous background, past perfect sequence; Light: used to / would

weeks.title: A goal and the next step
weeks.canDo: Describe an intention, name an arrangement, say what happens next and what you'll do if plans change.

grammar.main: going to for an intention; present continuous for a confirmed arrangement; will for a prediction or a decision made while speaking; present simple for timetables and ordinary future time clauses ('I'll apply when I finish'). An indirect question is different: 'I don't know when I'll finish'.
grammar.light: Conditionals 0–2 review. Zero for general truth, first for a real possibility, second for an unlikely or imagined situation.

sampleItems.prompt: I'll apply as soon as I ___ the course.
sampleItems.reason: 'As soon as' is a grammar cue here, not a vocabulary target.

sampleItems.prompt: I can't leave my job, but if I ___ more free time, I'd study full-time.

grammar.authoringNote: 'I will see my dentist tomorrow' is grammatical; don't flag it just because the visit is booked. Accept will or going to for predictions with present evidence. Conditional labels are teaching aids: accept natural variants such as 'when' in a zero conditional.

speaking.prompt: Share one goal, one step already arranged, what you'll do when that step is complete, and what you'll do if the plan changes.
speaking.model: My goal is to start a career in design. I intend to take a short course this spring, and I'm meeting someone from the college on Thursday. I'm looking forward to seeing some of the students' work. A friend who did the course has offered to help me choose a project. I think it'll be hard work, but it'll be worth it. When I finish the course, I'll apply for a few junior roles and use my project to show what I can do. If I don't get a place this spring, I'll take an evening class instead. And if I had more free time, I'd study full-time, but I need to keep working for now.
speaking.b2Stretch: Explain why the goal matters and weigh two alternatives, without the cue card.

writing.prompt: Write a message to a friend about a goal, a confirmed arrangement, your next step and a back-up plan. Use in order to once to explain a purpose.
writing.delayedRecall: You've decided to learn a new skill. What have you arranged, what will you do afterwards, and what will you do if it doesn't work out?

conversation.openingLine: So, any plans for the next few months?
conversation.learnerMoves: Give a goal, an arrangement and a next step; say what they'll do if it doesn't work out.
conversation.targetLanguage: Future forms, first and second conditionals; goal, intend to, career, look forward to

core.example: Her ambition is to run her own restaurant.
My goal is to start a career in design.
If you practise regularly, you'll achieve your goal.
We intend to move to the coast next year.
She's going to start a career in engineering.
The deadline for applications is 30 April.
She's going to apply for a job at the museum.
I'm looking forward to starting my new course.
He's determined to pass, so he's going to practise every day.

collocations.example: I'm working towards a degree in nursing.
I'll take the first step and contact the college.
This course will help you improve your skills.
Don't put off booking the course. With a pronoun: put it off.
I'm going to set myself a goal of reading one book a month.
We'll need to finish on Thursday to meet Friday's deadline.

families.card: ambitious on ambition; achievable recognition on achieve
achievement on achieve; achievable recognition only
one shared family card; successfully guided B2

vocabulary.note: Separate apply for a job from apply to an organisation. In look forward to, to is a preposition: use a noun or an -ing form. No future continuous (Week 14).

linkers.example: In order to save money, I'll cook at home.

checkpoint1.focus: Intention, arrangement, two ordinary future time clauses; Light: first vs second conditional

weeks.title: Agree on house rules
weeks.canDo: Say what is required, forbidden, optional or possible, ask and give permission, and offer advice.

grammar.main: have to for a requirement, mustn't for something forbidden, don't have to for optional; should for advice; can/can't now and could/couldn't for general past ability; 'Can/Could I...?' to ask permission and 'Yes, you can' / 'Sorry, you can't' to answer.
grammar.light: Question forms: auxiliary before subject ('What time do you usually get home?'), no do in subject questions ('Who takes the bins out?'), statement word order after 'Could you tell me...?'. Basic linkers: on the other hand, in fact, apart from that.

sampleItems.prompt: Taking turns cooking is optional. You ___ cook on Mondays.

grammar.authoringNote: For a specific past success use was able to or managed to, not could; couldn't works for a specific failure. Keep this contrast as a B2 note, not a scored item.

speaking.prompt: Welcome a new flatmate who arrives tomorrow: explain one shared responsibility, one rule and one optional routine, give one piece of advice, and end with a question for them. The live flatmate exchange is the conversation task.
speaking.model: Welcome to the flat! There are a few things you need to know. We have to clean up after cooking, and we mustn't leave the cooker on when we go out. You don't have to cook for everyone, but we usually eat together on Fridays. You can use the washing machine until ten. The neighbours can hear it through the wall, so if you need it later, please ask them politely first. I couldn't cook at all when I moved in, so don't worry if you're still learning. I think we should arrange a cleaning rota around our work hours. Apart from that, there's no fixed routine. We all get on with each other really well, so if you're not sure about something, just ask. What time do you usually get home, by the way?
speaking.b2Stretch: Add a likely problem (noise, guests, bills) and suggest a compromise, without the cue card.

writing.prompt: Write a welcome message for a new flatmate: one requirement, one rule, one optional thing and one piece of advice. Use at least one of the week's linkers (on the other hand, in fact, apart from that).
writing.delayedRecall: Tell a new colleague one thing they need to do, one thing they mustn't do and one thing that's optional.

conversation.openingLine: Hi! Is there anything I need to know about the kitchen?
conversation.learnerMoves: Explain a rule, answer a permission request ('Could I use the washing machine tonight?'), ask one question, suggest an arrangement.
conversation.targetLanguage: Obligation, ability and permission modals, question forms, linkers; get on with, arrange, routine, politely

core.example: You don't have to be close friends to get on with your colleagues.
Can we meet after work and catch up? Here: exchange news.
We should arrange to meet outside the station.
Try to stick to a routine during busy weeks.
You can rely on Maria to help if there's a problem.
We should talk and clear up the misunderstanding.
Can I invite some friends round on Saturday? BrE.
It was an awkward situation, but we managed to talk it through.
You can disagree politely.

collocations.example: We should make an effort to welcome new colleagues.
We have a lot in common: we both love cycling.
You should get in touch with the organiser.
Can you come over for coffee on Saturday?
You should keep a promise even if it's difficult.

families.card: reliable and unreliable on rely on; reliably recognition only

optional.example: Can I pop round after work? Informal BrE; short visit.

vocabulary.note: Pair get on with (relationship), catch up with (exchange news) and get in touch with (initiate contact). Week 3 linkers are the Light grammar point and required in the welcome-message writing task.

linkers.example: Living with friends can be fun. On the other hand, you have to share the housework.
We get on really well. In fact, we talk almost every day.
The bus was late. Apart from that, the day went well.

checkpoint1.focus: One item each for obligation, advice, ability and permission; Light: one question form

weeks.title: Give a short visitor guide
weeks.canDo: Describe customs and past facts with the passive, identify places and compare them.

grammar.main: be + past participle in present and past simple. Use the passive to focus on the place, event or result; add by + agent only if it matters. Contrast 'is held' with 'was built', and keep 'It happened' active.
grammar.light: Defining relative clauses with who, which, that and where; comparatives and superlatives including irregular better/best and worse/worst. Non-defining clauses are recognition only for now.

sampleItems.prompt: The craft market ___ in the main square every Sunday.
sampleItems.reason: Present passive for a regular event.

grammar.authoringNote: Use a guide-card cue such as 'Market hall / build / 1890' in controlled practice. In free speech accept natural active wording; don't require a set number of passives.

speaking.prompt: Record a 60–90 second guide for a first-time visitor. Include a regular event or custom, one fact about the past, one comparison and a recommendation. Don't require a set number of passives.
speaking.model: If you visit this town, start at the market hall. It was built in 1890, and the food market is held there every Saturday. It's a local tradition, and you can try food from nearby farms. It's the busiest place in town on a Saturday morning, so I'd set off early. There's also a local custom that surprises visitors: most shops are closed on Wednesday afternoons, so plan your shopping for another day. Afterwards, take a walk by the river. It's quieter than the centre, and it's the spot where I go to relax. The town isn't a famous destination, but it's one of the friendliest places I know.
speaking.b2Stretch: Add extra information with a non-defining clause, such as 'The market hall, which was built in 1890, ...'. Accept it, but don't require it.

writing.prompt: Write a visitor recommendation or trip note. Separate a place fact from what you personally did, and organise it with to begin with and all in all.
writing.delayedRecall: Introduce a venue in your neighbourhood. Say what normally takes place there, give one fact about its past and compare it with another place.

conversation.scenario: A weekend visitor asks for tips.
conversation.openingLine: I'm here for the weekend. What should I see?
conversation.learnerMoves: Recommend a place, give one fact about its past, compare it with another place, mention a custom.
conversation.targetLanguage: Passive, defining relative clauses, comparatives and superlatives; local, custom, destination, tradition, set off

core.example: Visitors are invited to take part in a local tradition.
The guide explained a local custom: visitors are asked to take off their shoes before they go inside.
It's one of the most popular holiday destinations on the coast.
We set off early to avoid the heavy traffic.
We were given a map to help us get around the city.
We were unfamiliar with the ticket system.
The hotel where we stayed had a welcoming atmosphere.
Local food is served in the hotel restaurant.

collocations.example: We took a guided tour of the old town.
We were encouraged to try the local food.
We travelled light because there wasn't much room for luggage.
We stopped overnight in York before driving on.
Our flight was delayed, so we missed our connection.

families.card: one productive family card; culturally recognition only

optional.example: We broke our journey with an overnight stay in York. Mainly BrE.

vocabulary.note: Keep passive models in present and past simple. Destination models a superlative and welcoming a defining relative clause. Local means 'from the area'; touristy is often disapproving.

linkers.example: To begin with, we were shown around the old town.
The hotel was comfortable. What's more, breakfast was included.
Despite the rain, the outdoor tour went ahead.
All in all, we had an excellent trip.

checkpoint1.focus: Two present passives and two past passives; Light: one relative clause or comparative/superlative
